content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a mixed and masked image modeling method (MixMIM) which is applied to vision transformers. Instead of replacing the masked patches with the special MASK symbol, MixMIM leverages the masked tokens from other images to avoid the inconsistency problem of training-finetuning. The paper reports good results, but I have major concerns according to the statement of the paper.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
    1. The question proposed in the paper, i.e., the training-finetuning inconsistency problem is a reasonable problem;
    2. The method proposed is applicable to various vision transformers

Weaknesses:
    1. In section 2.3, the paper notes that "Specifically, for each token, it is only allowed to aggregate information from the tokens belonging to the same image (group)", which implies that the implementation is CONTRARY to the insight of the paper. That is to say, the proposed method remains extracting features from the same MASKED image (which like MAE) instead of padding tokens from another image.
    2. The paper reports good results by pre-training for 600 epochs. However, according to the statement, the actual computation cost is up to FOUR times compared to MAE, which implies 600×4=2400 epochs. I think the performance gain comes from the more computational cost.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity is good
Quality is poor
Novelty is poor
Reproducibility is poor
content.summary_of_the_review: The study explores an interesting issue in masked image modeling. The implementation of the study is not consistent with the insight of the paper and the performance gain comes from heavy computation cost.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a masked image modeling (MIM) approach for self-supervised learning. Instead of using a learnable [MASK] token in the encoder input, it mixes the tokens of two (or more) images, then unmixes the encoder output, inserts the [MASK] tokens, decodes and reconstructs both (all) images. The paper also introduces a new variant of the Swin Transformer.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
- Well written
- Simple, interesting idea

Cons:
- Possibly limited or no novelty
- Unfair comparisons
- Weak performance
- Inappropriate metrics

The paper is very well written and a pleasure to read. The method is very simple and very clear. The idea is interesting in the sense that indeed the [MASK] token slows down the training process so it is more efficient to insert it after the encoder. There is a wide range of experiments, comparisons with state of the art and ablations.

After carefully reading the method and the ablation, the main contribution becomes unclear. In section 2.3, a "masked self-attention" strategy is proposed to reduce the difficulty of the task. This strategy is found the most effective in Table 10 and chosen by default. Unless I am mistaken, this means that the two (or more) input images are processed independently. But then, what is the difference from MAE? Especially when mixing 4 images, which is the default here, each has a masking ratio of 75%, exactly like the default of MAE. MAE also introduces the [MASK] token after the encoder. To me, it looks like processing 4 images with MAE in parallel is equivalent to processing one mix of 4 images with the proposed MixMIM, just presented in a different way. In this case, I can see no novelty.

The new variant of the architecture is irrelevant to the main contribution and I only see it as distraction. If a new architecture was meant as a main contribution, the paper should have been positioned accordingly, with relevant related work and comparisons as well as more tasks and supervision settings. I suggest to just remove it and focus on it in a different paper if needed.

What is unacceptable is to present results where MixMIM beats other MIM strategies by using a different architecture, e.g. Table 2 where 85.1 is made bold over the entire column and the related discussion. Even more unacceptable is to not present results on the same architecture at all, e.g. in Tables 4,5 for downstream tasks. Table 3 does compare fairly on a number of backbones, but only to one or two competitors and only on fine-tuning (see below).

The performance itself does not look competitive. In Table 1, with ViT-B at 600 epochs, MixMIM gives 67.0 linear probing accuracy, whereas iBOT Figure 12 gives >72.5 with ViT-S at 50 epochs. I disregard downstream tasks as explained above.

I do not find ImageNet fine-tuning accuracy appropriate as an evaluation metric alone, even though it is common nowadays, because differences between methods tend to be tiny and results tend to be inconsistent when comparing with other metrics. I suggest to add linear probing and k-NN to all experiments, and focus discussion on these metrics as well as downstream tasks on other datasets. ImageNet fine-tuning can remain for reference.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As discussed above, the writing and the overall implementation of this work is of very high quality and the method is simple and clear. However, unless I am missing something, the method appears to be equivalent to MAE, just presented differently. The originality needs to be clarified.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a simple and interesting strategy for MIM, well written and with lots of experiments. However, there is possibly no novelty and there are severe flaws in the experiments, including unfair comparisons between different models, inappropriate metrics and weak performance.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new masked image modeling framework called MixMIM, which mixes tokens from several images and discard the mask tokens in the encoder and reconstruct each image individually in the decoder part. MixMIM is applicable on several different architectures and achieves good results on several downstream tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- Extensive experiments and ablation study.
- Well written and easy to follow.

Weaknesses
- Due to the masked self-attention design, the mix operation does not appear to be informative. Especially considering MixMIM with ViT in 4 images with 0.75 ratio scenario (which is also the best setting from Table 8), MixMIM just acts like to concat four sparse image sequences (with the masked self-attention design to guarantee no information mixture between images) and feed into the MAE encoder, and then separately feed these four sparse image seq into the MAE decoder. The experiments also show that the performance (Table 2 and Table 3) and computational efficiency (Table 18) of MixMIM and MAE are very close on ViT-Base and ViT-Large.
- Some experimental comparisons are not fair. First, the normalized target introduced in MAE is also used in MixMIM, which will bring additional improvements. Second, MixMIM backbone uses larger window size (also means long sequence) compared to Swin, which will also bring expected improvements. As a result, these unfairness could introduce uncertainty in two important conclusions. The first is whether MixMIM still has significant efficiency gains and performance improvements compared to SimMIM. The second is whether MixMIM backbone performs better than Swin.
- Since efficiency is one purpose of MixMIM, the detailed comparison about computational cost / efficiency should be included in the experimental part, like in Table 2 and Table 3.
- The empirical evaluation provided in Appendix A.3. seems to be related to [1], and the connection to which should be discussed in this part.

[1] Revealing the Dark Secrets of Masked Image Modeling
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Good clarity and reproducibility.
- Please refer to the previous section for possible problems in quality and novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper provides better experiments and writing. However, the mixture operation was introduced into MIM only as a trick for increasing computational efficiency, which may limit the novelty of the paper. The subsequent experimental results and the possible problem of unfair comparison make the core claim of the paper even not necessarily valid.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new masked image modeling (MIM) method, MixMIM, for self-supervised learning. Specifically, the proposed method randomly generates a mask to mix two (or more) images, then uses a hierarchical vision transformer to encode the mixed image and a lightweight decoder to reconstruct the original images. Inside the encoder, masked self-attention is used to avoid interaction between patches from different images. The decoder takes the mask and the token embeddings to reconstruct the original images. The pre-trained encoder is then fine-tuned on different datasets for different downstream tasks, including image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation. Compared to the existing MIM method, the proposed method achieves better FLOPs/performance tradeoffs on these tasks. Ablation experiments are conducted to validate the design choices of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

- This paper proposed a new masked image modeling method MixMIM, combining the advantages of BEiT and MAE, two state-of-the-art MIM approaches, avoiding computation of [MASK] symbols and applicable to hierarchical backbones.
- Experiment comparison shows the proposed method achieves better FLOPs/performance tradeoffs on various downstream tasks after model fine-tuning.
- This paper conducted extensive experiments, which provided a better understanding of how well the proposed method work.

Weakness

- MixMIM uses masked self-attention to prevent the interaction of tokens from different images. What’s the difference compared to encoding two masked images separately and reconstructing them separately? If there is no interaction between two different groups of tokens, why mix them?
- Because MixMIM uses a mix of 4 images (Section 3) following a 75% masking ratio in MAE, is it equivalent to MAE training 4 times? In this case, MAE needs to be trained 4 times as long as the MixMIM for a fair comparison.
- Looking at Table 2, specifically comparing MAE and MixMIM, the results suggest that the performance is improved more from the backbone rather than mixing images. MAE and MixMIM using ViT-B achieve 83.6% and 83.8% top-1 accuracy, respectively, while MixMIM with MixMIM-B reaches 85.1%. Similar observations can be made in Table 4. Then we have to doubt: is mixing images necessary?
- The architecture of the decoder in MixMIM is not explained.
- Nitpick: MAE paper is published in CVPR 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is mostly well-written, with some technical details to be clarified.
The novelty of this paper is moderate by combining two state-of-the-art MIM methods: BEiT and MAE.
It would be plausible to reproduce the results, with more technical details clarified.
content.summary_of_the_review: MixMIM is a new method for self-supervised pre-training and does achieve comparable performance or better FLOPs/performance tradeoffs. However, the necessity of the mixing operation is not well supported by the experiment results. The backbone change contributes more to performance improvement.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
